title: One slow phone can slow down your whole Wi-Fi
description:
Wi-Fi gives every device an equal turn to send its next packet, not equal time. A phone far from the router drops to a slow rate (in the classic 802.11b case, from 11 to 1 megabit a second), so each of its packets holds the air about 12 milliseconds instead of 1. With 3 fast laptops and that one slow phone, the phone takes three quarters of the air and every device ends up at about 0.6 megabits a second, slower than the phone's own rate. With the phone close by, each would get about 1.9. This is the 802.11 "performance anomaly" (Heusse et al., INFOCOM 2003); routers with airtime fairness fix it by sharing time instead of turns (Høiland-Jørgensen et al., USENIX ATC 2017).

Numbers checked in code (verify.py): the paper's throughput model plus a 200,000-packet simulation of Wi-Fi's random backoff.

social_caption: One phone far from your router can slow every device on your Wi-Fi to below its own speed. Here's the turn-taking math behind it.
facts_checked: 802.11b hosts drop from 11 to 5.5, 2 or 1 Mb/s when far/faded; a 1 Mb/s host cuts all 11 Mb/s hosts below 1 Mb/s; CSMA/CA gives equal long-term channel access; a 1 Mb/s host holds the channel 11x longer (Heusse, Rousseau, Berger-Sabbatel, Duda, 'Performance anomaly of 802.11b', INFOCOM 2003, https://www.csd.uoc.gr/~hy439/reading/list_2011/10.1.1.12.3822.pdf)
1534-byte frame: 1.12 ms at 11 Mb/s, 12.27 ms at 1 Mb/s (12.9 ms with overhead); one round of 3 fast + 1 slow = 17 ms; slow share 75% (verify.py)
Eq. 7, N = 4: all fast 1.93 Mb/s each; 3 fast + 1 slow 0.61 Mb/s each, a 69% drop; simulation of 200,000 backoff contests: 0.602-0.608 Mb/s for every device (verify.py)

The performance anomaly still limits modern WiFi; an airtime-fairness scheduler at the access point fixes it, accepted into the mainline Linux kernel (Høiland-Jørgensen et al., 'Ending the Anomaly', USENIX ATC 2017, https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.00064)

beats.say: One slow phone on your Wi-Fi drags every device down to its speed.
It's not hogging your data. It's just far from the router.
Out there, it drops from 11 megabits a second to 1. Your 3 laptops stay at 11.
Wi-Fi shares the air by turns. Every device gets an equal shot at sending its next packet.
At 11 megabits, a packet is on the air for about a millisecond. At 1 megabit, 12.
Equal turns sound fair. Now watch your laptop.
Each round, your laptops take a millisecond each. Then everyone waits 12 for the phone. Three quarters of the air, one phone.
With the phone close, each device got 1.9 megabits. Now every device gets 0.6. Slower than the phone's own 1.
Equal turns, unequal time. Your slowest device sets everyone's speed. That's why some routers now share by time, not turns.
